title: ASASSN-14ko timing permits constant orbital decay if emission delays vary by at least seven days under stated error bounds
abstract: We test whether flare timing alone excludes steady orbital decay in ASASSN-14ko. We use 23 optical rise and Swift UV timing estimates from a prior SCI study. A linear program fits the epoch, initial period and marker offset while it minimizes the range of a common emission delay. At a fixed period derivative of -0.0026, the minimum range is 7.007 days for intervals of plus or minus twice the reported error with a one-day floor in quadrature. A contrast of three optical rise times cancels epoch and period and proves the same lower bound. A feasible delay history attains it. Adding 21 published peak estimates raises the bound to 9.692 days under a shared-delay assumption. A three-day error floor reduces the primary bound to zero. Fixed-delay forecast failures therefore need not exclude constant orbital decay. We give conditional future rise-time envelopes for specified delay caps. This is a method and a reanalysis of existing timing products, not new photometry or a physical model of delay. The bounds depend on marker stability and the assumed error intervals.

display.caption: Minimum delay range against fixed orbital period derivative, and feasible delay histories at -0.0026. Timing intervals use twice the reported error with a one-day floor in quadrature. These are feasibility bounds, not confidence intervals.
